pl-l3d21c1-d1e117.summary: Introduces the question that follows from the preceding: whether in death the soul or the flesh was separated from the Word.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e120.summary: Presents the opinion that the flesh was divided from the divinity in death as it was from the soul. If the divinity united the flesh to itself through the soul, separating the flesh from the soul separated it from the divinity; and the soul was separated in death, else death would not have been true, since, per Augustine, death is the separation of soul from flesh.
claims: Some hold that the flesh was separated from the divinity in Christ's death.
Their argument relies on the soul mediating the union of flesh to Word.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e126.summary: Notes that the proponents add an authority to their probable argument.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e130.summary: Gives their authority: Ambrose comments on the cry of dereliction that the man cries out as he is about to die by separation from the divinity, since death could not be present unless life, which is the divinity, withdrew. They apply this to the flesh's separation from God.
claims: Ambrose seems to say that the divinity withdrew from the man in death.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e142.summary: Replies that this separation must be understood as the dereliction is. Christ cried out that he was forsaken while still alive, so if forsaking meant dissolved union, he would have been man and not God while living, which no one says. God forsook him by exposing him to his persecutors for a time and not exercising power to defend him: the divinity withdrew protection, not union, absent outwardly for defense but present inwardly for union. The scapegoat sent into the desert while the other goat is sacrificed figures this: the humanity immolated, the divinity 'went into the desert', heaven, by restraining its power, as Hesychius explains.
claims: God's forsaking of Christ was a withdrawal of protection, not of union.
If forsaking meant dissolution, Christ would have been mere man while still alive.
The divinity restrained its power so the passion could be accomplished.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e160.summary: Concludes that Ambrose's words must be taken in the sense just given.
claims: Ambrose's statement refers to withdrawal of protection.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e163.summary: Introduces a second group who rely on authority to claim that the divinity withdrew from the man as to the flesh in death.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e166.summary: Gives their authority: Athanasius anathematizes anyone who does not confess that the whole man assumed by the Son of God, 'assumed anew' or freed, rose on the third day. They infer that what was assumed anew in the resurrection had been set aside in death.
claims: Some argue from Athanasius that the man was set aside in death and reassumed.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e172.summary: Replies that if 'assumed anew' meant union, it would apply to the whole man, soul and flesh, since Athanasius says 'whole man'; so the soul too would have been set aside in death, which only an enemy of truth would say. Yet unless they grant this, the authority does not support them.
claims: The opponents' reading would imply the soul was separated from the Word, which is absurd.
The authority speaks of the whole man, not the flesh alone.
concepts: union of soul with the Word

pl-l3d21c1-d1e176.summary: Explains Athanasius's intent: he wrote against those who denied Christ's resurrection, thinking he was held by death. 'Whole man assumed anew' means that Christ joined soul again to body and truly lived as man in them as before death.
claims: Athanasius's 'assumed anew' means the reuniting of soul and body.
Athanasius wrote against deniers of the resurrection.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e185.summary: States the solution: in death the soul was separated from the flesh, which is why Christ truly died, but neither from the Word. Augustine on 'I lay down my life' teaches that the soul did not lay itself down, nor did the Word lay down soul or flesh; the flesh laid down the soul, but by the power of the deity remaining in it.
claims: In Christ's death soul was separated from flesh, but neither from the Word.
The flesh laid down the soul by the power of the indwelling deity.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e200.summary: Quotes Augustine: the Word never laid down the soul; the flesh laid it down in expiring and rose when it returned. Death separated flesh and soul for a time, but neither from the Word. Lombard notes that this plainly teaches the union was in no way dissolved.
claims: The union of the Word with soul and flesh was not dissolved in death.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e209.summary: Adds Augustine against Felicianus: Christ felt death by sharing human affection he freely took, but did not lose the power by which he gives life to all; he did not desert his flesh in the tomb, as he formed it in the Virgin's womb. Lombard draws out that Christ did not abandon his flesh in death, that life did not depart from him, and that he gave up his spirit freely.
claims: Christ did not desert his flesh in the tomb.
Christ's divine life and power were not lost in death.
Christ gave up his spirit freely.

pl-l3d21c1-d1e221.summary: Confirms with Ambrose: Christ emitted his spirit and did not lose it, as arbiter of his body; he sent it from the flesh to the Father.
claims: Christ emitted, not lost, his spirit.

pl-l3d21c1.summary: Asks whether, in Christ's death, the soul or the flesh was separated from the Word. Some argue that the flesh was severed from the divinity, since it was united through the soul, and cite Ambrose ('the man cries out as he dies by separation from the divinity') and Athanasius (the whole man 'assumed anew' in the resurrection). Lombard answers that the divinity withdrew its protection, not the union, leaving the man to his persecutors, as the scapegoat went into the desert; and that if Athanasius meant reunion, the soul too would have been set aside, which no one holds. Athanasius was opposing those who denied the resurrection. Augustine and Ambrose teach that death separated soul from flesh but neither from the Word, and that Christ laid down his soul by his own power.
claims: In death neither Christ's soul nor his flesh was separated from the Word.
The divinity's 'separation' or 'forsaking' means withdrawal of protection, not dissolution of union.
Athanasius's 'assumed anew' refers to the reuniting of soul and body in the resurrection.
Christ laid down his soul by the power of the indwelling divinity, not under compulsion.
